C005.subject: Amazon rainforest dieback threshold
C005.object: the mean distance between forest fragments exceeds a critical value of 15 km, independent of total deforestation extent, due to disruption of seed dispersal and microclimate buffering
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Amazon rainforest dieback threshold the mean distance between forest fragments exceeds a critical value of 15 km, independent of total deforestation extent, due to disruption of seed dispersal and microclimate buffering]

[PATH:empirical] Empirical analysis of seed dispersal networks and forest fragment spatial configuration across Amazonian landscapes using remote sensing (e.g., Landsat-derived fragmentation metrics) and field-based seed rain data — Directly tests the causal mechanism: whether mean fragment distance >15 km reduces seed dispersal effectiveness and seedling recruitment, independent of total deforestation area.

[PATH:theoretical] High-resolution regional climate model (RCM) simulations comparing microclimate variables (temperature, humidity, wind speed) in landscapes with varying fragment distances, holding total forest cover constant — Evaluates the microclimate buffering disruption claim by isolating the effect of fragment spacing on edge-related microclimate changes, controlling for deforestation extent.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on Amazon forest fragmentation thresholds (e.g., from the Biological Dynamics of Forest Fragments Project and Large-Scale Biosphere-Atmosphere Experiment) focusing on fragment distance metrics and ecosystem function — Synthesizes prior empirical and modeling work to identify whether a 15 km critical distance emerges across different datasets and to assess independence from total deforestation.

qualifier.temporal: mid-21st century projections under moderate climate change scenarios

C006.subject: Amazon rainforest dieback threshold

evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Amazon rainforest dieback threshold total edge length, rather than the mean distance between forest fragments, when deforestation extent exceeds 30% of the basin]

[PATH:empirical] High-resolution satellite imagery analysis (e.g., Landsat, Sentinel-2) of the Brazilian Amazon basin under >30% deforestation, measuring total edge length vs. mean fragment distance and correlating with observed forest dieback events (e.g., increased fire frequency, canopy mortality). — Directly tests whether edge length outperforms fragment distance as a predictor of dieback thresholds in real landscapes, using spatially explicit historical data.

[PATH:theoretical] Spatially explicit ecosystem model simulations (e.g., LPJmL, ED2) parameterized for the Amazon, systematically varying deforestation patterns to isolate the effects of total edge length and mean fragment distance on hydrological and carbon cycle feedbacks under current climate conditions. — Provides controlled, mechanistic tests of the hypothesis by manipulating landscape metrics independently, complementing observational data with causal inference.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing literature on Amazon fragmentation effects (e.g., from the Biological Dynamics of Forest Fragments Project, INPE deforestation databases) focusing on studies that report both edge length and fragment isolation metrics in relation to ecological degradation. — Synthesizes prior empirical findings to assess consistency of the edge-length vs. distance hypothesis across multiple studies and scales, identifying potential confounding factors.

[PATH:empirical] High-resolution remote sensing analysis of forest fragment shapes and edge-effect mortality in the Brazilian arc of deforestation (e.g., using Landsat or Sentinel data combined with field plot data on tree mortality) — Directly tests the hypothesis by comparing the predictive power of edge-to-area ratio variance versus total edge length on observed tree mortality rates in fragments where deforestation exceeds 30% basin-wide.

[PATH:theoretical] Dynamic global vegetation model (DGVM) simulations that explicitly parameterize edge effects as a function of fragment shape complexity (e.g., ED2, LPJ-GUESS with sub-grid fragmentation) — Allows controlled experiments to isolate the effect of edge-to-area ratio variance on dieback thresholds under current climate and land-use scenarios, providing mechanistic support or refutation.

qualifier.temporal: post-2000, under current climate and land-use scenarios
qualifier.geographic: Brazilian Amazon, specifically the arc of deforestation

[PATH:empirical] Landscape-scale fragmentation experiments in the Brazilian Amazon, e.g., the Biological Dynamics of Forest Fragments Project (BDFFP) long-term data on fragment isolation effects on forest biomass and microclimate — Directly tests whether mean distance between fragments (isolation) drives dieback thresholds more than edge length, using empirical measurements of forest dynamics in fragments of known spatial configuration.

[PATH:theoretical] Spatially explicit simulation models that vary both edge length and fragment distance independently under >30% deforestation scenarios, e.g., using the INLAND or LPJmL dynamic vegetation model coupled with a landscape connectivity module — Allows controlled manipulation of the two fragmentation metrics to isolate their relative influence on dieback thresholds, addressing the hypothesis mechanistically.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of remote sensing studies on Amazon forest degradation (e.g., from PRODES and DETER data) that quantify edge effects versus isolation effects on canopy moisture stress and fire incidence — Synthesizes existing observational evidence across the region to evaluate whether fragment distance consistently predicts dieback beyond edge length effects in real landscapes.

[PATH:empirical] High-resolution satellite imagery analysis (e.g., Landsat, Sentinel-2) combined with basin-wide deforestation maps (e.g., PRODES) to compute fragment size distributions and inter-fragment distances across regions exceeding 40% deforestation, then correlate with field-measured or remote-sensed indicators of forest dieback (e.g., canopy moisture stress, fire frequency, tree mortality). — Directly tests the hypothesis by comparing the predictive power of fragment size variance versus mean inter-fragment distance on actual dieback patterns in high-deforestation areas.

[PATH:theoretical] Spatially explicit simulation experiments using a landscape-scale forest dynamics model (e.g., FORMIND, LPJ-GUESS) that systematically varies fragment size distributions and inter-fragment distances while holding deforestation extent constant at >40%, measuring emergent dieback thresholds. — Isolates the causal effect of each spatial metric on dieback, controlling for confounding variables, and can identify nonlinear interactions between fragment size variance and deforestation extent.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis and literature review of existing studies on Amazon fragmentation thresholds (e.g., Laurance et al. 2011, Ewers & Didham 2006, and recent edge-effect studies) that report fragment size and distance metrics in relation to forest degradation or dieback, re-analyzing data to compare variance vs. mean effects. — Leverages existing datasets to provide a cost-effective, broad-scale test; if consistent patterns emerge across multiple studies, it strengthens the hypothesis; if not, it suggests the need for new empirical work.
